survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 financial literacy data for 15-year-old students and applies the OECD-recommended complex survey procedures. Specifically, it reports using final student weights together with balanced repeated replication (BRR) replicate weights to obtain correct standard errors under the multilevel sampling design. The analysis also incorporates the PISA plausible values (10 PVs) for the standardized administrative scores, and it standardizes outcomes using each country’s mean and standard deviation. The paper does not describe any additional ML-specific weighting; instead, it follows PISA best practices for estimation and variance estimation, and includes missing-flag variables to avoid dropping observations.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that it uses PISA recommended practices including plausible values and missing-flag variables, but it does not explicitly describe the missing-data handling rule for item nonresponse (e.g., whether cases are listwise deleted, imputed, or retained via PV procedures). Because the dependent variables are PV-based standardized administrative scores, missingness is likely handled through the PISA PV framework and the inclusion of missing flags, but the exact rule is not fully documented in the text provided. This is therefore a reporting gap for the missing-data mechanism beyond the missing-flag approach.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is restricted to PISA 2018 participants who are 15-year-old students in the 20 countries that administered the PISA financial literacy assessment. The study constructs four binary indicators of whether students encountered specific types of financial education problems at school (during mathematics class; during another class; one-off lesson/activity from an outside visitor in school time; extra-curricular activity outside school time). Outcomes are standardized administrative scores for financial literacy and mathematics, and the student fixed-effects specification pools each student across the two subjects (financial literacy vs mathematics) and differences within-student across subjects. The paper also includes missing-flag variables to avoid losing observations, and it uses PISA recommended practices (final student weights, BRR replicate weights, and plausible values).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Financial Literacy (15-year-olds) — student fixed-effects across Financial Literacy vs Mathematics
main_findings.performance_metrics: Student fixed-effects (equation 4). Effect of financial education during mathematics class on financial literacy (vs mathematics) ranges from 0.12 to 0.37 SD across countries; significant positive coefficients reported in Table 1 for several countries (e.g., Bulgaria: 0.17; Brazil: 0.21; Canada: 0.34; Chile: 0.12; Estonia: 0.41; Finland: 0.26; Georgia: 0.20; Italy: 0.27; Lithuania: 0.22; Spain: 0.16; USA: 0.16). Non-positive/insignificant cases include Netherlands (−0.01), Peru (−0.03), Serbia (−0.06), and Slovak Republic (−0.04) for the math-class modality in Table 1.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Financial Literacy data for 15-year-old students in 20 countries, the study leveraged financial education in mathematics class together with mathematics benchmark level and student background controls (gender, immigrant status, socioeconomic status, grade retention) to predict financial literacy (standardized administrative score) in a student fixed-effects framework. It found that financial education encountered during mathematics classes is associated with higher financial literacy, with effects ranging from about 0.12 to 0.37 standard deviations depending on the country, while other modalities (other class; one-off outside visitor; extracurricular) generally do not show positive improvements. This indicates that integrating economics/financial literacy content into mathematics instruction may be a more effective policy lever than relying on stand-alone or extracurricular financial education formats, though the authors interpret results as conditional associations rather than definitive causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The paper analyzes the relationship between financial education and financial literacy using PISA 2018 financial literacy data for 15-year-old students in 20 countries (Bulgaria, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Estonia, Finland, Georgia, Indonesia, Italy, Lithuania, Latvia, Netherlands, Peru, Poland, Portugal, Russia, Serbia, Slovak Republic, Spain, USA). It estimates a student fixed-effects model that differences each student’s standardized administrative scores between financial literacy and mathematics, using PISA recommended practices: final student weights, balanced repeated replication (BRR) replicate weights, and 10 plausible values. In the main fixed-effects results (Table 1, equation 4), financial education encountered during mathematics classes is associated with higher financial literacy in most countries, with effects reported from roughly 0.12 to 0.37 SD depending on the country, while other delivery modalities show no consistent positive gains. The study cautions that unobserved confounding may remain and that the financial education exposure is self-reported, so findings should be interpreted as conditional associations rather than fully causal impacts.
